name: Zoe Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I lead nine people who handle orders and service problems for a big packaging company. I start with the overnight exceptions, then work out which problems need a person and which need a better process. I like helping a junior colleague untangle a difficult customer call. I don't like spending Friday evening explaining a target that changed on Thursday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into the lead role so young, and what is home like after those Fridays?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an MBA while working and got good at the messy cases, so they promoted me twice. I share a flat with my partner, Luis, who works shifts at a hotel; we have no children. My salary is low for this level, and the MBA loan and rent mean we have less than a month's expenses saved. There are very few companies this size near us, so leaving isn't a quick fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to use a tool if it genuinely clears a queue, but not to promise miracles. The boring problems with returns and missing stock are still ours to solve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved about the job, but the rent and my MBA loan don't disappear. At our pay, even a quiet month feels like standing on a narrow ledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month, I'd keep running the morning exception meeting and review the team's returns figures each Friday. In the first year, I'd put 80 a month into savings if Luis's hotel shifts hold and keep paying the minimum on my MBA loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a relief to picture my work carrying on. I'm still uneasy about our bills, because nothing in that picture makes our cushion thicker by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in a month when Luis loses a hotel shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings transfer would be the first thing I pause. I'd rather do that than miss rent, and I'd tell Luis before the month starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relieved and worried at once. Which part follows you home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan does. AI Plateau leaves my job standing, but it doesn't pay my MBA loan for me.

say: I'd use **small tools** that clear a queue without promising a miracle.
I'd keep the team's **returns work** in human hands.
think: I'm relieved my **job** keeps its shape.
My **rent and loan** still leave little room for a bad month.
do: Keep the **morning meeting** and Friday returns review through the first year.
Save **80 a month** when Luis's shifts allow it.
feel: I feel **relief** about work and unease about bills.
S0.quote: AI Plateau leaves my job standing, but it doesn't pay my MBA loan for me.
fieldNote: Her **work** feels secure in this picture.
Thin **savings** keep household money on her mind despite relief.
Her **Friday reviews** remain routine, so the scenario offers no career change.

steps.text: Keep the morning exception meeting and review returns figures each Friday
Transfer 80 a month to savings when Luis's hotel shifts allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should check the quality before moving customers to a bot. The team deserves to know which tasks are changing, not just get a new target on a Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work is heavy on checking and answering customers, so I think the company would stop replacing leavers. A manager with half a team might be next on the chart, even if I can run that team well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my director for a month-long trial of AI drafting replies, with me checking errors against the actual order record. In the first year, I'd document which difficult cases still need a person and move 50 a month from takeaways into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, because doing the trial well could make our team smaller. I also want the evidence in my hands rather than wait for somebody else's slide deck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the team comes to mind when you say smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, the newest service worker, takes the routine order questions. I'd try to train her on the hard disputes before those routine calls dry up, though I can't promise her a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the team you are worried about your own role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them the trial might change headcount, but I wouldn’t make my own fear their burden. I don’t want to demonstrate an AI tool that removes my own management job.

say: I'd demand **quality checks** before customers move to a bot.
I'd tell staff which **tasks change** before targets change.
think: Routine calls may disappear, taking **team posts** with them.
A smaller team could put **my role** on the chart.
do: Run a **one-month trial** of drafted replies against order records.
Train Marta on **difficult disputes** and save 50 a month from takeaways.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shrinking the team I lead.
S1.quote: I don’t want to demonstrate an AI tool that removes my own management job.
fieldNote: She wants **trial evidence** before changing service work.
She discusses staff risks openly but keeps **personal fear** private.
Her concern for **Marta** makes the task trial a staff decision, not merely a cost exercise.

steps.text: Test AI drafted replies for one month against actual order records
Transfer 50 a month from the takeaway budget into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our company needs to tell people plainly what happens to their jobs. I wouldn't pretend that a fast new system leaves a service office untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work is nearly all of my day, so 2028 feels like a direct deadline for my role. Luis's hotel work might last until the robots arrive around 2031, but our rent needs both incomes now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd sit with Luis and map rent, loan payments and the smallest food budget we could manage. Before 2028, I'd ask HR in writing about severance and move the MBA loan onto any cheaper lawful repayment plan; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd apply for the few local training and service roles still posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed. I can make a list, but two years is not long enough to rebuild our savings and my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes from that budget first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cancel the weekend rail trips to see friends and stop eating out. I wouldn't cut the rent payment and hope the landlord understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if HR has no answer about severance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a dated written answer and speak with colleagues about asking together. A neat spreadsheet can't make two paychecks appear.

say: I'd ask for a **plain job plan** from the company.
I wouldn't promise a service office survives **2028 AGI** untouched.
think: Most of **my day** is thinking work exposed in 2028.
Luis's hotel income may last until **2031 robots**, but rent needs two paychecks.
do: Map **rent and loan** payments with Luis this week, then cancel rail trips and meals out.
Ask **HR about severance** before 2028 and apply for local roles after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a two-year deadline and thin savings.
S2.quote: A neat spreadsheet can't make two paychecks appear.
fieldNote: Her **office work** faces thinking AI in 2028, before hotel robots in 2031.
She seeks written **severance terms** while cutting specific costs.
She distinguishes **2028 office risk** from Luis’s later possible exposure in hotel work.

steps.text: Cancel weekend rail trips and restaurant meals to protect rent payments
Apply for locally posted training and service roles in the first year after 2028 AGI
Ask colleagues to seek a dated severance answer together if HR stays silent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a company time to offer a real path for people, not a farewell meeting. I'd want a published timetable for which service tasks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably pay down the MBA loan before my management job changes, if my pay holds. I still wouldn't build a future around being the person who approves a machine's decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in January, I'd ask payroll to take an extra 100 a month toward the loan, provided rent is covered. I'd take the company's training course on customer dispute law, then in the first year after 2031 apply for compliance roles that handle appeals when an automated answer is contested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the five years give me time to qualify for work I could explain to a hiring manager. The robots coming around 2034 worry me less than the thinking system in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if that compliance course doesn't lead to a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not quit my job for a certificate. I'd check actual postings twice a month and ask the course tutor which employers have hired graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that work in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already handle the calls that become formal complaints. Five years gives me a route out of the approvals chair, but only if a real vacancy exists.

say: I'd call for a published **task timetable** and a real path for staff.
Five years gives the company time to make **offers** before cuts.
think: I might clear the **MBA loan** before my role changes.
I don't want to live by approving a **machine's decisions**.
do: Pay an extra **100 monthly** toward the MBA loan if rent is covered.
Take a **dispute law course** and apply for posted compliance roles after 2031.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years gives me a route to qualify.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a route out of the approvals chair, but only if a real vacancy exists.
fieldNote: She ties training to **actual vacancies**, avoiding a speculative leap.
The **2031 thinking system** matters more to her than 2034 robots.
She will **check postings** twice monthly before counting on a new field.

steps.text: Pay an extra 100 a month toward the MBA loan when rent is covered
Complete the company course on customer dispute law before 2031
Apply for posted compliance appeal roles in the first year after 2031 AGI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to negotiate a fair transition and test what the machines really do. I wouldn't tell a 20-year-old joining the team that management is a safe lifetime ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough time to finish the loan and build a cushion, if Luis and I keep working. It also gives me a chance to move into work that needs a person on the other side of a complaint, though I don't know how long that lasts after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd make a ten-year debt and savings plan with Luis, starting with a 100 monthly loan overpayment when shifts permit. I'd shadow our complaints team one afternoon a month and apply for a posted appeals supervisor role before 2036; in the first year after AGI, I'd stay in that role only if the firm still funds human appeals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than cornered. The dates are still unsettling, but a decade lets me test whether that other role actually exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the appeals work also disappears, what is your next move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the cushion for a search, not burn it on a second degree with no openings attached. I'd look beyond this town if the local postings dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luis about the plan tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the first job is paying down what we owe and getting room to choose. A ten-year warning is useful only if we put dates on the calendar.

say: I'd ask for a **fair transition** tested over time.
I wouldn't sell management as a **lifetime ladder** to new staff.
think: A decade could clear our **loan** and build savings.
Even human appeals may face **uncertainty** after 2036.
I may need to **search beyond town** if local openings dry up.
do: Make a **ten-year plan** with Luis and overpay the loan when shifts permit.
Shadow the **complaints team** monthly and apply for an open appeals supervisor role.
Keep the **appeals role** after 2036 only while the firm funds human review.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with enough time to test another role.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is useful only if we put dates on the calendar.
fieldNote: She uses the longer runway for **debt and savings** first.
Her career move depends on **funded human appeals** after 2036.
The **local market** remains narrow even with ten years to prepare.

steps.text: Overpay the MBA loan by 100 monthly when Luis's shifts permit
Shadow the complaints team one afternoon each month
Apply for a posted appeals supervisor role before 2036 AGI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my job is thinking work and the rent needs both of us. A written severance rule, paid time to train and honest dates for cuts would help more than another cheerful town hall. I could make choices if I knew what money and time we had.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask who checks an AI answer when a customer has lost a shipment. My team currently owns lost-shipment mistakes; whoever takes the job next needs a name and a phone number, not just a dashboard.

headlineQuote: My team currently owns lost-shipment mistakes; whoever takes the job next needs a name and a phone number, not just a dashboard.
portrait: **Zoe**, 27, is a skilled team lead with an MBA and lower pay for her level.
Her household has **less than a month** saved while paying rent and an MBA loan.
She tests tools against **real orders** and moves only toward posted roles.
A **2028 deadline** alarms her; five or ten years lets her pay debt and explore appeals work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens her thinking-heavy management job before she can rebuild savings.
whatWouldHelp: A written **severance rule**, paid training time and honest dates for cuts would let her plan.
